3 Day a Week Marathon Training Plan

This 3 day a week marathon training plan is for runners who can only run three times a week, or whose bodies cope better with fewer runs. It assumes you currently run 15–20 miles (24–32 km) a week. Over 16 weeks you run three purposeful sessions a week: a threshold or marathon-pace run, an interval or marathon-pace run, and a long run. Two cross-training sessions add aerobic work without extra impact. Every week is listed below in miles and kilometres, with a pace key and guidance on adjusting the plan.

Peak running volume is 30 miles (48 km), with a 20-mile (32 km) long run four weeks before the race. Not sure which plan? Compare them here.

Who this plan is for

  • You can run three days a week and cross-train (cycle, swim, row or use an elliptical) on two more.
  • You currently run 15–20 miles (24–32 km) a week, with a long run of 7–8 miles (11–13 km).
  • You are time-limited, injury-prone, or an older runner who recovers better with days off between runs.
  • Your race is 16 weeks away.

Is this your first marathon, and could you manage a fourth short run? The beginner plan uses four runs and an easier build. Starting from under 15 miles a week? Begin with the 6 month plan.

The full 16-week schedule (miles & km)

With three runs, none of them can be "junk". Run 1 is threshold or MP work. Run 2 is intervals or MP. Run 3 is the long run. Put at least one day between runs, for example Tuesday, Thursday and Sunday, and do your cross-training on two of the other days. Weekly totals count running only.

Pace key

  • Easy: conversational, about 60–90 s/mi (35–55 s/km) slower than goal marathon pace.
  • Long run: easy pace, 45–90 s/mi (30–55 s/km) slower than goal marathon pace, except segments marked @ MP.
  • MP: your goal marathon pace.
  • T (threshold): comfortably hard, the pace you could race for about an hour. Roughly 25–40 s/mi (15–25 s/km) faster than MP. Jog 2 min between reps.
  • I (intervals): 5K–10K effort, roughly 50–80 s/mi (30–50 s/km) faster than MP. Jog 90 s–2 min between reps.
  • Hills: 60 s uphill at 5K effort; jog back down.
  • Strides: 20 s quick and relaxed at the end of an easy run. Walk back to recover.
  • Workout distances include a 1–2 mi (2–3 km) warm-up and cool-down.

How the 16 weeks are built

  • Weeks 1–4: 17–21 miles (27–34 km) of running, two 30-minute cross-training sessions, and a long run that grows from 8 to 10 miles (13 to 16 km).
  • Weeks 5–8: longer threshold and interval sessions, and the first MP runs. Long runs reach 14 miles (23 km).
  • Weeks 9–13: long runs of 15, 17, then 20 miles (24, 27, 32 km), with a cutback in week 11. Cross-training rises to 45–60 minutes.
  • Weeks 14–16: taper, at 23, 19 and 7 miles of running (37, 31 and 11 km) plus lighter cross-training.

Weekly running mileage never rises by more than about 12%, and there is a cutback in weeks 4, 8 and 11.

Making three runs a week work

  • Cross-training is part of the plan. Keep it at an easy, conversational effort. It builds aerobic fitness and doesn't need to be hard.
  • Protect the long run. If you must miss a run, miss Run 2 rather than the long run.
  • Pace realistically. With lower mileage, the final 10K of the marathon is usually the hardest part. Base your goal pace on a recent half marathon (about 2.1 × your half time) and add 5–10 minutes.
  • Adding a day: if your schedule frees up, add a 30–40 minute easy run in place of one cross-training session.
  • Pain or injury: pain that changes how you run, or doesn't ease within a few days, means stop and see a doctor or physio. Don't run through it.

Fueling, strength and race week

Strength training twice a week matters even more on low running mileage, because it helps your legs handle the impact of race day. Practise taking carbohydrate on every long run from week 7. More detail is in our guide to what a marathon plan should include.

FAQ

Can you train for a marathon running 3 days a week?

Yes. Three quality runs plus two cross-training sessions is enough for many runners to finish a marathon well, especially if they have a few months of consistent running behind them before they start.

Is 3 days a week enough for a first marathon?

It can be. If you have never run a marathon, the 20-mile long run in week 12 is the key test, and you should be able to finish it comfortably. Newer runners who can fit in a fourth short run will usually find the beginner plan easier to absorb.

What counts as cross-training in a 3 day marathon plan?

Any sustained, low-impact cardio: cycling, swimming, rowing, the elliptical or brisk uphill walking. Aim for 30–60 minutes at an easy effort. Strength training is extra and doesn't replace these sessions.

Can you run a sub-4 marathon on 3 days a week?

Some runners do, usually ones with a strong aerobic base. If sub-4 is your main goal and you can run more often, the sub 4 hour plan gives you a better chance.
keyTakeaway: Three runs a week can get you to a marathon if each one has a job: a threshold or marathon-pace run, an interval session and a long run, plus two easy cross-training sessions.
